summary: Provides a framework for usage feedback in COPS-PR. The COPS protocol can report success, failure and accounting information to a Policy Decision Point, and this document focuses on accounting reports, meaning monitoring and reporting how much an installed policy state is used.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network applies a rule, the controller may want to know how much it was used. This note describes how devices report that back.

questions: how does cops-pr report policy usage
what is an accounting timer in cops
how does a device report usage on shared objects

subtitle: How network devices report usage of applied policies

tldr.problem: Network policy systems apply rules to traffic, but the policy decision maker needs to know how much each rule is actually being used.
tldr.mechanism: The COPS-PR protocol lets enforcement devices send periodic reports back to the policy controller, describing what happened to each applied policy rule during a monitoring interval.
tldr.outcome: This framework enables policy controllers to make smarter decisions by learning how their rules were used.

today: RFC 3483 is an informational document that describes a framework for implementing usage feedback in COPS-PR deployments. It has not been obsoleted and continues to serve as a reference for policy-based network management systems.

sections.title: Policy Feedback Basics
sections.content:
The COPS (Common Open Policy Services) protocol lets a policy decision point, or PDP, push policy rules down to enforcement points on the network, called PEPs. This framework describes how PEPs report usage back to the PDP: which rules were triggered, how many times, whether they succeeded or failed. A multimedia session controller, for example, might install quality-of-service rules on a router, then need usage data to decide whether to allow more sessions or adjust the rules.

This document focuses specifically on accounting reports, meaning periodic reports of how much the policy was used, as opposed to simple success or failure messages. The framework defines three things: which objects are monitored, what metrics are collected, and when reports are delivered.
sections.plainLanguage: A policy controller sends rules to a device, then the device regularly reports back: here is how much traffic hit this rule, how many packets passed or were dropped, and when.

sections.title: Three Components of the Framework
sections.content:
The framework describes three layers of policy that work together. First, a selection criteria policy decides which objects on the device to monitor — for example, all IP filters on interface 1, or a dropper queue. Second, a usage feedback class specifies which metrics to collect for those objects, such as packet count, byte count, or drop count. Third, a linkage policy binds the selection criteria to the usage class and says when reports should be delivered: periodically, on demand, when a threshold is reached, or only if the values change.

The device monitors and tracks usage as policy is installed. The PDP controller collects reports and can use the data to adjust policy, coordinate with billing systems, or simply audit what is happening on the network. When the controller wants an immediate report outside the normal interval, it can solicit one and the device responds right away.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller picks what to measure (a rule), how to measure it (packet count), and when to hear about it (every minute). The device then sends reports on that schedule.

sections.title: Periodic Reporting and Intervals
sections.content:
Usage feedback is normally periodic and unsolicited: the device sends reports at intervals set by the controller. The controller specifies a minimum interval in an Accounting Timer during connection setup, pacing how often the device can send reports. The device can be instructed to stop reporting while still monitoring (useful when the controller is overwhelmed), or to stop both monitoring and reporting (saving device resources).

Reports may be triggered not only by time but also by reaching a configured threshold value, or by detecting a change in the data. When the controller wants to check usage in the middle of an interval, it can send a solicit message and receive immediate feedback.

If the device context switches (moving from one installed policy set to another), the current usage is reported for the old context before activating the new one. This ensures no data is lost during transitions.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller says "send me reports every 60 seconds," and the device counts traffic and sends updates. If something important happens sooner, the controller can ask for an immediate report.

sections.title: Shared Objects and Failover
sections.content:
Some objects on a device are shared among multiple uses. For example, one IP filter might apply to traffic on multiple ports. The framework handles this by allowing the selection criteria and usage feedback classes to share the burden of identifying exactly which object instance generated the report. The selection criteria might specify an IP address, and the usage class might add a port number to uniquely identify the flow.

If the connection between device and controller fails, the device continues to monitor and track usage as long as the policy remains valid in the cache. Once cached policy expires, monitoring stops. When the connection is restored and the device is still caching policy, the controller signals that the device may resume reporting. The device then sends all accumulated usage data and resumes normal periodic reporting.
sections.plainLanguage: If the connection breaks, the device keeps track locally. When reconnected, it sends all the data it collected while offline.
